claim: Synaptotagmin binds Ca2+ through its two C2 domains to trigger membrane interactions.
source: The synaptic vesicle Ca2+ sensor Synaptotagmin binds Ca2+ through its two C2 domains to trigger membrane interactions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of Synaptotagmin.

claim: Mutations in the C2B domain Ca2+-binding pocket dominantly disrupt release from invertebrates to humans.
source: mutations in the C2B domain Ca2+-binding pocket dominantly disrupt release from invertebrates to humans
evidence: This observation is stated in the abstract and supported by references to prior work in the introduction.

claim: An intragenic suppressor screen for Synaptotagmin C2B Ca2+-binding mutants in Drosophila uncovered essential residues within Synaptotagmin.
source: We performed an intragenic screen for suppressors of lethality induced by expression of Synaptotagmin C2B Ca2+-binding mutants in Drosophila. This screen uncovered essential residues within Synaptotagmin
evidence: The screen methodology and results are described in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: A C2B surface implicated in SNARE complex interaction is required for rapid synchronization and Ca2+ cooperativity of vesicle release.
source: a C2B surface implicated in SNARE complex interaction that is required for rapid synchronization and Ca2+ cooperativity of vesicle release
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data presented in the results.

claim: Synaptotagmin 1 functions as the Ca2+ sensor for driving synchronous fusion of synaptic vesicles following an action potential.
source: Synaptotagmin 1 (Syt1) functions as the Ca2+ sensor for driving synchronous fusion of synaptic vesicles following an action potential (Geppert et al., 1994; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Syt1 is tethered to synaptic vesicles through a single transmembrane domain and contains two cytosolic Ca2+ binding C2 domains.
source: Syt1 is tethered to synaptic vesicles through a single transmembrane domain and contains two cytosolic Ca2+ binding C2 domains (Perin et al., 1990).
evidence: This structural description is provided in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The C2 domains contain Ca2+-binding loops that insert into negatively charged lipid bilayers following Ca2+ influx.
source: The C2 domains, termed C2A and C2B, contain Ca2+-binding loops that emerge from the top of each domain and insert into negatively charged lipid bilayers following Ca2+ influx (Chapman and Davis, 1998; Chapman and Jahn, 1994; Davletov and Südhof, 1993; Desai et al., 2000; Fernandez et al., 2001).
evidence: This mechanism is described in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Syt1 can interact with the SNARE complex, with several studies suggesting an important role for this interaction during fusion.
source: Syt1 can interact with the SNARE complex, with several studies suggesting an important role for this interaction during fusion (Bennett et al., 1992; Brewer et al., 2015; Chicka et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010; Li et al., 1995; Littleton et al., 2001; Lynch et al., 2008; Lyubimov et al., 2016; Pang et al., 2006; Schupp et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with extensive citations supporting the interaction.

claim: Not all studies support a Syt1-SNARE binding mechanism during release.
source: However, not all studies support a Syt1-SNARE binding mechanism during release (Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This contrasting view is noted in the introduction with citations.

claim: Syt1 contains a Ca2+-independent lipid-binding surface on one side of the C2B domain.
source: Syt1 also contains a Ca2+-independent lipid-binding surface on one side of the C2B domain that represents a candidate mechanism for docking Syt1 on the plasma membrane, potentially positioning the Ca2+ binding loops near sites where fusion will occur (Bai et al., 2004; Kuo et al., 2009; Loewen et al., 2006; Mackler and Reist, 2001; Pérez-Lara et al., 2016; Rickman et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2016; Young and Neher, 2009).
evidence: This property is described in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Syt1 undergoes multimerization.
source: In addition, Syt1 undergoes multimerization (Chapman et al., 1998; Fukuda and Mikoshiba, 2000; Lee et al., 2013; Littleton et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2003; Zanetti et al., 2016)
evidence: This property is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: It is unknown whether a Syt1 monomer or oligomer represents the active state of the protein.
source: though it is unknown whether a Syt1 monomer or oligomer represents the active state of the protein.
evidence: This gap in knowledge is explicitly stated in the introduction.

claim: Syt1 copy number per vesicle ranges from 7 to 15.
source: Syt1 is abundant on synaptic vesicles, with estimates of the copy number per vesicle ranging from 7 to 15 (Mutch et al., 2011; Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: This quantitative estimate is provided in the introduction with citations.

claim: Ca2+ binding to the Syt1 C2B domain is a critical step required for fast synchronous release.
source: Prior work identified Ca2+ binding to the Syt1 C2B domain as a critical step required for fast synchronous release, with Ca2+ binding to C2A playing an important but more modulatory role in the process (Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2013; Mackler et al., 2002; Nishiki and Augustine, 2004; Shin et al., 2009; Yoshihara et al., 2010).
evidence: This finding from prior work is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The C2B Ca2+ binding pocket contains five negatively charged aspartate residues (D1 to D5) that help coordinate binding of multiple Ca2+ ions.
source: The C2B Ca2+ binding pocket emerges from the top of the domain and contains five negatively charged aspartate residues (numbered D1 to D5) that help coordinate binding of multiple Ca2+ ions (Fernandez et al., 2001).
evidence: This structural detail is provided in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Drosophila strains with mutations in one or more of the D1 to D5 residues in the C2B Ca2+ binding pocket result in a dominant-negative phenotype.
source: Drosophila strains with mutations in one or more of the D1 to D5 residues in the C2B Ca2+ binding pocket result in a dominant-negative (DN) phenotype, disrupting neurotransmission even in the presence of wildtype Syt1 (Lee et al., 2013; Mackler et al., 2002; Yoshihara et al., 2010).
evidence: This genetic observation is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Autosomal dominant mutations in the Ca2+ binding pocket of the C2B domain of human Syt2 result in an autosomal-dominant disorder presenting with peripheral neuropathy and dysfunctional synaptic transmission at neuromuscular junctions.
source: More recently, we identified autosomal dominant mutations in the Ca2+ binding pocket of the C2B domain of human Syt2, a Syt1 homolog enriched in the PNS, that result in an autosomal-dominant disorder presenting with peripheral neuropathy and dysfunctional synaptic transmission at neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) (Herrmann et al., 2014; Whittaker et al., 2015).
evidence: This clinical finding is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: An autosomal-dominant mutation in the Syt1 C2B domain has been found in a patient presenting with a more severe neurodevelopmental disorder.
source: An autosomal-dominant mutation in the Syt1 C2B domain has also been found in a patient presenting with a more severe neurodevelopmental disorder (Baker et al., 2015).
evidence: This clinical case is mentioned in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of UAS-Syt1C2BD1,2N or UAS-Syt1C2BD3,4N transgenes with elavC155 GAL4 in wildtype Drosophila causes late pupal lethality.
source: Pan-neuronal overexpression of UAS-Syt1C2BD356N,D362N (referred to hereafter as Syt1C2BD1,2N) or UAS-Syt1C2BD416N,D418N (referred to hereafter as Syt1C2BD3,D4N) transgenes with elavC155 GAL4 in otherwise wildtype Drosophila with two endogenous copies of native Syt1 causes late pupal lethality.
evidence: This experimental result is described in the results section.

claim: Overexpression of DN Syt1 resulted in a strong suppression of the evoked response, reducing the evoked excitatory junctional current (eEJC) by 86% compared to controls.
source: Overexpression of DN Syt1 resulted in a strong suppression of the evoked response, reducing the evoked excitatory junctional current (eEJC) by 86% compared to controls (white) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This quantitative result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Overexpression of wildtype Syt1 lacking C2B Ca2+ binding mutations did not reduce eEJCs.
source: In contrast, overexpression of wildtype Syt1 lacking these mutations did not reduce eEJCs.
evidence: This control result is stated in the results section.

claim: The C2B DN mutations enhanced the rate of spontaneous fusion, increasing mini frequency more than two-fold.
source: In addition to the strong suppression of synchronous evoked release, the C2B DN mutations also enhanced the rate of spontaneous fusion, increasing mini frequency more than two-fold (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The screen identified 105 mutations that produced viable progeny.
source: We screened over 500,000 F1 offspring and identified 105 mutations that produced viable progeny (Table 1).
evidence: This screening result is stated in the text and detailed in Table 1.

claim: 54 of the viable lines contained a premature stop codon within the Syt1 transgene.
source: Sequence analysis confirmed 54 of the viable lines contained a premature stop codon that was induced by EMS within the Syt1 transgene
evidence: This sequencing result is stated in the results section.

claim: 22 point mutations present throughout the C2A and C2B domains resulted in amino acid substitutions that led to viable progeny.
source: In addition to these stop codons, we identified an additional 22 point mutations present throughout the C2A and C2B domains that resulted in amino acid substitutions that led to viable progeny (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: Over half of the point mutations identified reduced expression when assayed by Western blotting.
source: Over half of the point mutations identified reduced expression when assayed by Western blotting, suggesting they alter protein stability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ten amino acid substitutions identified in multiple suppressor lines did not alter the levels of DN Syt1 protein.
source: Ten of the remaining amino acid substitutions identified in multiple suppressor lines did not alter the levels of DN Syt1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two hits to residue D229N in the C2A Ca2+ binding pocket were identified that disrupt C2A Ca2+ binding.
source: We identified several residue changes within the C2A domain that rescued viability (Table 1), including two hits to a previously characterized residue in the C2A Ca2+ binding pocket (D229N) that disrupts C2A Ca2+ binding (Robinson et al., 2002).
evidence: This result is stated in the text with a citation and shown in Table 1.

claim: Overexpression of Syt1 with mutations in both the C2A and C2B Ca2+ binding sites did not cause dominant-negative defects in release.
source: We previously found that overexpression of Syt1 with mutations in both the C2A and C2B Ca2+ binding sites did not cause dominant-negative defects in release (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This prior result is stated with a citation.

claim: Intact Ca2+ binding by C2A is required for the DN effects of the C2B domain mutations within Drosophila.
source: Together with the C2A D229N hits from this screen, these data indicate that intact Ca2+ binding by C2A is required for the DN effects of the C2B domain mutations within Drosophila.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the genetic data.

claim: Dual mutations in C2A and C2B do disrupt release in mammalian Syt1.
source: This contrasts with observations for DN mammalian Syt1, where dual mutations in C2A and C2B do disrupt release (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This contrasting observation is stated with a citation.

claim: Three C2A suppressor mutations altered residue R250 located at the interface between the C2A and C2B domains.
source: Beyond the C2A Ca2+ binding pocket, three C2A suppressor mutations altered residue R250 (R250H, R250C) located at the interface between the C2A and C2B domains, and near the site of a potential dimer interface from the crystal structure (Figure 2A).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The R250H mutation completely suppressed the DN effects, with a full recovery of the evoked response to control levels.
source: The R250H mutation completely suppressed the DN effects, with a full recovery of the evoked response to control levels (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The R250H mutation did not significantly rescue the enhanced spontaneous release.
source: In contrast, the R250H mutation did not significantly rescue the enhanced spontaneous release (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four suppressors mapped onto the polybasic surface of the C2B domain, including K379E and T381.
source: A second group of four suppressors were identified that map onto the polybasic surface of the C2B domain, including K379E and T381﻿ (Figure 2E).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The K379 residue has been suggested to function in Ca2+ independent lipid binding that may pre-position Syt1 on the plasma membrane prior to fusion.
source: The K379 residue in particular has been suggested to function in Ca2+ independent lipid binding that may pre-position Syt1 on the plasma membrane prior to fusion (Loewen et al., 2006; Rickman et al., 2004), and as part of a secondary SNARE binding surface (Brewer et al., 2015).
evidence: This proposed function is stated with citations.

claim: The K379E mutation resulted in a partial suppression of the evoked response defect.
source: The K379E mutation resulted in a partial suppression of the evoked response defect (Figure 2F–G)
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: The K379E mutation had no significant effect on the enhanced spontaneous release.
source: but had no significant effect on the enhanced spontaneous release (Figure 2H).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Two mutations in P363 were identified that map next to the C2B D2 Ca2+ binding residue.
source: A third category of suppressors was defined by two mutations in P363 (P363S), which maps next to the C2B D2 (D362) Ca2+ binding reside (Figure 2I).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: A mutation in the homologous residue (P308L) in human Syt2 has been found to cause an autosomal-dominant form of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome.
source: A mutation in the homologous residue (P308L) in human Syt2 has been found to cause an autosomal-dominant form of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome in a multigenerational UK family (Herrmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This clinical finding is stated with a citation.

claim: The P363S mutation partially suppressed the defective evoked response following expression of C2BD1,2N.
source: The P363S mutation partially suppressed the defective evoked response following expression of C2BD1,2N (Figure 2J–K)
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2J-K.

claim: The P363S mutation had no significant effect on the enhanced spontaneous release.
source: and had no significant effect on the enhanced spontaneous release (Fig, 2L).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: 19 suppressor mutations disrupted five amino acids (S332, R334, E348, Y391 and A455) that decorate a C2B domain surface opposite from the polybasic region.
source: A final group of suppressor mutations identified in the screen mapped to a poorly characterized side of the C2B surface on the opposite face from the polybasic region (Figure 2M). We identified 19 suppressor mutations that disrupted five amino acids (S332, R334, E348, Y391 and A455) that decorate this C2B domain surface.
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2M.

claim: These five residues (S332, R334, E348, Y391 and A455) contribute to the primary interface surface formed between the C2B domain and the SNARE complex.
source: A recent structure of the SNARE complex bound to Syt1 (Zhou et al., 2015) indicates these five residues contribute to the primary interface surface formed between the C2B domain and the SNARE complex (see below).
evidence: This structural interpretation is stated with a citation.

claim: The R334H change completely suppressed the ability of the C2BD1,2N mutant to disrupt evoked release.
source: The R334H change completely suppressed the ability of the C2BD1,2N mutant to disrupt evoked release, while S332L partially suppressed the evoked defect (Figure 2M–O).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2M-O.

claim: S332L partially suppressed the evoked defect caused by C2BD1,2N.
source: The R334H change completely suppressed the ability of the C2BD1,2N mutant to disrupt evoked release, while S332L partially suppressed the evoked defect (Figure 2M–O).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2M-O.

claim: Neither R334H nor S332L mutation was capable of significantly suppressing the increased spontaneous release observed following expression of C2BD1,2N.
source: Neither mutation was capable of significantly suppressing the increased spontaneous release observed following expression of C2BD1,2N (Figure 2P).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2P.

claim: Overexpression of transgenes harboring R250H, K379E, P363S, S332L or R334H mutations in the absence of the C2B Ca2+ binding mutation failed to cause a dominant disruption of synaptic transmission.
source: In contrast to the ability of Syt1C2BD1,2N to dominantly disrupt release, overexpression of transgenes harboring each of the mutations described above (R250H, K379E, P363S, S332L and R334H) in the absence of the C2B Ca2+ binding mutation failed to cause a dominant disruption of synaptic transmission on their own (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the absence of Syt1, synchronous synaptic vesicle release is dramatically reduced at Drosophila NMJs.
source: In the absence of Syt1, multiple defects in neurotransmitter release occur at Drosophila NMJs. Synchronous synaptic vesicle release is dramatically reduced, asynchronous release is increased, and spontaneous fusion rates rise (Broadie et al., 1994; DiAntonio and Schwarz, 1994; Littleton et al., 1994; 1993; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citations.

claim: In the absence of Syt1, asynchronous release is increased at Drosophila NMJs.
source: In the absence of Syt1, multiple defects in neurotransmitter release occur at Drosophila NMJs. Synchronous synaptic vesicle release is dramatically reduced, asynchronous release is increased, and spontaneous fusion rates rise (Broadie et al., 1994; DiAntonio and Schwarz, 1994; Littleton et al., 1994; 1993; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citations.

claim: In the absence of Syt1, spontaneous fusion rates rise at Drosophila NMJs.
source: In the absence of Syt1, multiple defects in neurotransmitter release occur at Drosophila NMJs. Synchronous synaptic vesicle release is dramatically reduced, asynchronous release is increased, and spontaneous fusion rates rise (Broadie et al., 1994; DiAntonio and Schwarz, 1994; Littleton et al., 1994; 1993; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citations.

claim: In the absence of Syt1, there are defects in synaptic vesicle docking at Drosophila NMJs.
source: In addition, there are defects in synaptic vesicle docking (Reist et al., 1998), endocytosis (Littleton et al., 2001; Poskanzer et al., 2006; 2003) and Ca2+ cooperativity of fusion (Littleton et al., 1994; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citations.

claim: In the absence of Syt1, there are defects in endocytosis at Drosophila NMJs.
source: In addition, there are defects in synaptic vesicle docking (Reist et al., 1998), endocytosis (Littleton et al., 2001; Poskanzer et al., 2006; 2003) and Ca2+ cooperativity of fusion (Littleton et al., 1994; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citations.

claim: In the absence of Syt1, there are defects in Ca2+ cooperativity of fusion at Drosophila NMJs.
source: In addition, there are defects in synaptic vesicle docking (Reist et al., 1998), endocytosis (Littleton et al., 2001; Poskanzer et al., 2006; 2003) and Ca2+ cooperativity of fusion (Littleton et al., 1994; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citations.

claim: The R250H Syt1 transgene rescued several aspects of the null phenotype.
source: The R250H Syt1 transgene rescued several aspects of the null phenotype, indicating interactions regulated by this residue are not absolutely essential for Syt1 function, consistent with the behavioral rescue we observed.
evidence: This result is stated in the text.

claim: Evoked neurotransmitter release was decreased by 60% in the R250H mutant compared to WT Syt1 transgenic rescues.
source: However, evoked neurotransmitter release was decreased by 60% compared to WT Syt1 transgenic rescues (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This quantitative result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Release in the R250H mutant was synchronous with little asynchronous fusion observed.
source: While fusion is largely asynchronous in syt1 null mutants, release in the R250H mutant was synchronous with little asynchronous fusion observed (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: The R250H mutation had a significant increase in mini frequency compared to controls and null mutants.
source: The R250H mutation had a surprising effect on spontaneous release, with a significant increase in mini frequency compared to controls and null mutants (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: R250-mediated interactions play a role in clamping spontaneous release, but do not participate in suppressing the enhanced asynchronous fusion events observed in syt1 nulls.
source: As such, interactions mediated by R250 play a role in clamping spontaneous release, but do not participate in suppressing the enhanced asynchronous fusion events observed in syt1 nulls.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental results.

claim: Independent interactions regulate the inhibitory properties of Syt1 on spontaneous versus asynchronous release.
source: The divergent effects on suppression of spontaneous versus asynchronous release indicate that independent interactions regulate these inhibitory properties of Syt1.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental results.

claim: R250-mediated interactions are important for triggering normal amounts of vesicle fusion during an evoked response, but are not as critical for the timing of fusion.
source: We conclude that R250-mediated interactions are important for triggering normal amounts of vesicle fusion during an evoked response, but are not as critical for the timing of fusion.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental results.

claim: The R199 residue (homologous to Drosophila R250) is positioned at interface of the C2A and C2B domains in mammalian Syt1.
source: The R199 residue, which is homologous to Drosophila R250, is positioned at interface of the C2A and C2B domains (Figure 1J, Figure 2A).
evidence: This structural observation is stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The domains of native Syt1 remain relatively stable during microsecond-scale MD simulations, though minor conformational transitions were observed.
source: The MD trajectory (Figure 4A–D) demonstrated that the domains remain relatively stable, though minor conformational transitions were observed.
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The organization of Syt1 observed by crystallography with perpendicularly oriented and tightly interacting domains is likely to be stable in solution.
source: These results suggest that although Syt1 is likely to undergo minor conformational rearrangements in solution, the organization observed by crystallography with perpendicularly oriented and tightly interacting domains is likely to be stable.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the MD simulation results.

claim: In the final state of the Syt1 trajectory, R199 is positioned at the interface of the tightly interacting C2A and C2B domains.
source: Interestingly, in the final state of the Syt1 trajectory, R199 is positioned at the interface of the tightly interacting C2A and C2B domains (Figure 4E).
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The R199H mutation drastically destabilized the Syt1 inter-domain organization.
source: Strikingly, the mutation drastically destabilized the Syt1 inter-domain organization.
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text.

claim: The mutated R199H Syt1 structure had an increased gyration radius, indicating a larger separation of the C2 domains.
source: Importantly, the mutated Syt1 structure had an increased gyration radius (Figure 4H,L), indicating a larger separation of the C2 domains likely causes the conformational transitions.
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4H,L.

claim: The Syt1 dimer remained stable during 2.8 µs MD simulation and underwent only subtle rearrangements of the loop regions.
source: We found the dimer remained stable and underwent only subtle rearrangements of the loop regions, but inter-domain and monomer re-arrangement did not occur (Figure 5A)
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The dimer was stabilized by hydrophobic interactions of R199, which formed a salt bridge with N207 and tight hydrophobic contacts with V205.
source: The dimer was stabilized by hydrophobic interactions of R199, which formed a salt bridge with N207 and tight hydrophobic contacts with V205 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Syt1 dimer structure observed by crystallography is likely to be stable in solution and not an artifact of crystallization.
source: The MD stimulation of the Syt1 dimer suggest the structure observed by crystallography is likely to be stable in solution and not an artifact of crystallization.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the MD simulation results.

claim: In the Syt1 dimer model on the plasma membrane, the C2B polybasic stretch from residues 321 to 327 of both Syt1 monomers engaged the lipid bilayer, positioning the C2B Ca2+ binding loops oriented towards the plasma membrane.
source: Notably, the C2B polybasic stretch from residues 321 to 327 (KELKKKK) of both Syt1 monomers engaged the lipid bilayer, positioning the C2B Ca2+ binding loops oriented towards the plasma membrane (Figure 5C).
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the Syt1 dimer model, the Ca2+ binding loops of the C2A domains emerged from the opposite side of the structure, indicating they may interact with the synaptic vesicle lipid bilayer rather than the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, the Ca2+ binding loops of the C2A domains emerged from the opposite side of the structure, indicating they may interact with the synaptic vesicle lipid bilayer rather than the plasma membrane.
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text.

claim: The Syt1 dimer could act as an intermediate in the fusion pathway by stabilizing a state with the synaptic vesicle and the plasma membrane in close proximity, but not merging, thus inhibiting spontaneous fusion.
source: Such an arrangement suggests a model whereby the Syt1 dimer could act as an intermediate in the fusion pathway. We hypothesize that the Syt1 dimer could stabilize a state with the synaptic vesicle and the plasma membrane in close proximity, but not merging, thus inhibiting spontaneous fusion.
evidence: This model is proposed based on the computational results.

claim: Ca2+ binding would induce penetration of the C2B domains into the plasma membrane and penetration of the C2A domains into the vesicle membrane, bridging the two membranes to create tension and promote stalk formation and fusion pore opening.
source: Ca2+ binding would then induce penetration of the C2B domains into the plasma membrane and penetration of the C2A domains into the vesicle membrane, bridging the two membranes to create tension and promote stalk formation and fusion pore opening.
evidence: This mechanism is proposed based on the computational model.

claim: MD simulations of the mutated Syt1 dimer showed that dimer structure and organization was substantially disrupted.
source: To test this prediction directly, we performed MD simulations of the mutated Syt1 dimer and observed that dimer structure and organization was substantially disrupted (Figure 5D).
evidence: This computational result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Although dimerization may still occur in the R250H mutant background, the dimer structure observed for native Syt1 would be less stable.
source: This result suggests that although dimerization may still occur in the R250H mutant background, the dimer structure observed for native Syt1 would be less stable.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The K379E mutation had only modest effects on wildtype Syt1 activity and was able to significantly rescue the lethality observed in the syt1 null mutant.
source: In contrast to the robust ability of the K379E mutation to disrupt the dominant-negative effects of the C2B Ca2+ binding mutants on fusion, the mutation had only modest effects on wildtype Syt1 activity and was able to significantly rescue the lethality observed in the syt1 null mutant.
evidence: This result is stated in the text.

claim: Release in the K379E mutation background was synchronous, with little asynchronous release observed.
source: Release in the K379E mutation background was synchronous, with little asynchronous release observed (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A-F.

claim: The primary defect in K379E was a ~ 50% reduction in the evoked EJC amplitude.
source: The primary defect identified was a ~ 50% reduction in the evoked EJC amplitude (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: K379 regulates the total amount of vesicles that fuse, but does not play a critical role in release timing or the suppression of asynchronous release.
source: indicating K379 regulates the total amount of vesicles that fuse, but does not play a critical role in release timing or the suppression of asynchronous release.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental results.

claim: The K379E mutation did not rescue the enhanced spontaneous neurotransmitter release observed in the null mutant.
source: The K379E mutation did not rescue the enhanced spontaneous neurotransmitter release observed in the null mutant (Figure 6G).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The polybasic motif in the C2B domain promotes normal levels of synaptic vesicle release, but is not essential for the process and does not play an important role in suppressing asynchronous fusion.
source: We conclude that the polybasic motif in the C2B domain promotes normal levels of synaptic vesicle release, but is not essential for the process and does not play an important role in suppressing asynchronous fusion.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental results.

claim: The P363S mutation resulted in a severe reduction in evoked EJC amplitude.
source: The P363S mutation resulted in a severe reduction in evoked EJC amplitude (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The P363S mutation altered synchronous versus asynchronous components of release, with the amount of asynchronous release dramatically increased similar to the null mutant.
source: as well as altering synchronous versus asynchronous components of release (Figure 6C–F). Similar to the null mutant, the amount of asynchronous release was dramatically increased (Figure 6C,D,F).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: The P363S transgene largely rescued the enhanced spontaneous release observed in the null mutant.
source: The P363S transgene largely rescued the enhanced spontaneous release observed in the null mutant (Figure 6E)
evidence: This result is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Residue P363 does not play a major role in helping Syt1 function as a clamp for spontaneous release.
source: suggesting this residue does not play a major role in helping Syt1 function as a clamp for spontaneous release.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental results.

claim: Residues S332 and R334 decorate the primary interface of the Syt1-SNARE binding surface.
